content: UQCRC2, also referred to as QCR2, UQCR2, or MC3DN5, is a protein encoded by the UQCRC2 gene in humans. This protein is a subunit of the respiratory chain protein ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase, also known as Complex III or the cytochrome b-c1 complex. The cytochrome b-c1 complex is composed of the product of one mitochondrially encoded gene, MTCYTB (mitochondrial cytochrome b), and ten nuclear genes, including UQCRC1, UQCRC2, cytochrome c1, UQCRFS1 (Rieske protein), UQCRB, 11 kDa protein, UQCRH (cyt c1 hinge protein), Rieske protein presequence, cyt. c1 associated protein, and Rieske-associated protein. Mutations in the UQCRC2 gene are associated with mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 5. The UQCRC2 protein is composed of 453 amino acids, has a molecular weight of approximately 4 kDa, and contains 14 exons. It belongs to the peptidase M16 family and the UQCRC2/QCR2 subfamily. Additionally, UQCRC2 has a transit peptide domain, which is essential for its mitochondrial localization. The ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase (b-c1 complex) consists of 11 subunits, including three respiratory subunits (cytochrome b, cytochrome c1, and Rieske/UQCRFS1), two core proteins (UQCRC1/QCR1 and UQCRC2/QCR2), and six low-molecular-weight proteins (UQCRH/QCR6, UQCRB/QCR7, UQCRQ/QCR8, UQCR10/QCR9, UQCR11/QCR10, and a cleavage product of Rieske/UQCRFS1). UQCRC2 is part of the hydrophobic core of the b-c1 complex and is critical for the stabilization of ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase. Function The protein encoded by the UQCRC2 gene is localized in the mitochondrion, where it is a component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase complex (Complex III). This complex is an integral part of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. The core protein UQCRC2 is essential for the assembly and stabilization of the complex. Clinical Significance Variants in the UQCRC2 gene have been linked to mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 5. This condition is a disorder of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and presents with a highly variable phenotype depending on the affected tissues. Clinical manifestations include mitochondrial encephalopathy, psychomotor retardation, ataxia, severe failure to thrive, liver dysfunction, renal tubulopathy, muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, lactic acidosis, and hypoglycemia. Homozygous mutations leading to an arginine-to-tryptophan substitution at position 183 have been associated with mitochondrial complex III deficiency due to UQCRC2 dysfunction. The inheritance pattern is proposed to be autosomal recessive. Interactions UQCRC2 has been identified to participate in 98 protein-protein interactions, with 90 of these being co-complex interactions. Proteins such as CAC1A, QCR1, UQCRC1, CACNA1A, STOM, a8k1f4, HLA-B, ARF6, and Mapk3 have been found to interact with UQCRC2.
